1. Open the starwars dataset (located in tidyverse)
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
data(starwars)
```

2. Create a scatter plot of character's height and mass. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass)) + geom_point()
```

2a. Change the color and shape of the points in your scatter plot. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass)) + geom_point(shape = 10, color = "violet")
```

3. Add Homeworld as a third variable to your scatterplot. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass, color = homeworld)) + geom_point(shape = 10)
```

3a. What do you notice about the graph? (e.g. describe what you see)

I noticed that since colors consists of gradient of colors and some colors only differ being a bit darker or lighter, it is hard to distinguish what homeworld each point represents


4. Make a boxplot of height. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height)) + geom_boxplot()
```

5. Make a boxplot of height for each species present in the data. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, species)) + geom_boxplot() 
```

5a. change the appearance of your graph in at least 3 ways. 
```{r}
library(viridis)
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, species)) + geom_boxplot() + theme_classic() + labs(x = "Height", y = "Species", title = "Starwars Character Height by Species") + theme(text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12))
```

6. Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph that uses a color palette from viridis.
```{r}
library(viridis)
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass, color = sex)) + geom_point() + scale_color_brewer(palette = "Reds")

```
